narrative: The model estimated a 47% chance that you will leave your job in the near term. Although that is close to a coin flip rather than a certainty, it is high enough to be treated as a retention risk, which is why the promotion decision went against you. The strongest factor in the assessment was your total years of experience: at 1–5 years, you sit in the most common range among employees predicted to stay, and this factor pushed the estimate toward staying. However, two factors outweighed it. You reported having other job opportunities while in this role; only about one in four employees predicted to stay had such opportunities, so this strongly increased the leave signal. Working in the “other” sector also added risk, since that sector is less common among stayers, at about one in five. The result is not a judgment of your performance but a warning that external options and sector context may make departure more likely. Before revisiting promotion, discuss your career path, what opportunities would keep you engaged, and whether the role can offer clearer advancement. The organization should also consider a retention plan and check whether the promotion denial itself affects your engagement.
